paras: The reported lynching of Charles Young was a killing said to have taken place near Coal City, St. Clair County, Alabama, on the night of Saturday, November 7, 1903, after Young, a Black railroad construction worker, was accused of attempting to assault a white woman, Mrs. Barbour. The story, which came secondhand through Ragland, ran in papers from Maine to Montana in the following days. The Birmingham Age-Herald, however, stated that the St. Clair County lynching reported in distant papers never took place.

According to a Birmingham dispatch, Young worked at a railroad construction camp on the Seaboard Air Line near Coal City. The Montgomery Advertiser described Mrs. Barbour as the wife of "a respected citizen" of the county.

The Associated Press version, dated Ragland, November 9, said Mrs. Barbour was alone at home when Young entered the house and that her screams frightened him away. The Montgomery Advertiser gave a milder account of the alleged offense, saying Young went to the Barbour home, asked for something, and finding Mrs. Barbour alone was "said to have offered insult." By that paper's report he "was chased, found and lynched," a statement it qualified as coming from "the reports which come from" the place.

No report named the men who killed Young, gave their number, or described the method or the place beyond "near Coal City." Only headlines such as "Negro Strung Up" and "Negro Hangs High" suggested a hanging.

No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage. On November 12 the Birmingham Age-Herald, in an editorial titled "News by Anticipation," said the lynching "not only did not take place, but was not even considered," and argued that under Governor William Dorsey Jelks a lyncher would face jail, indictment and trial.

Coverage came almost entirely from one short wire item that opened, in its fullest form, with the words "A report has reached here from Coal City." Some papers dropped that qualifier and stated the lynching as fact, among them the New Haven Daily Morning Journal and Courier and the Savannah Morning News. The brief ran on November 10 in the Wichita Daily Eagle, the St. Louis Republic, the Richmond Times Dispatch, the Worcester Spy under the head "The Daily Lynching," and the Daily Kennebec Journal, and on November 13 in the Wilmington Semi-Weekly Messenger and the Newberry Herald and News. The Butte Inter Mountain printed it under "Negro Hangs High" with the place garbled as "Colorado City."

Headlines took the accusation as the cause, as in the Paducah Sun's "Negro Strung Up for Attempting to Criminally Assault a White Woman." The Birmingham Age-Herald, by contrast, faulted rural correspondents for anticipating lynchings and declared that "no one is lynched in the law-abiding state of Alabama," without naming Young or questioning the accusation against him. No coverage in the Black press was found.

Whether Young was killed is disputed: every report of the lynching passed on an unconfirmed account from Coal City, while the Age-Herald, a Birmingham paper writing two days later, denied it. The editorial did not name Young or Coal City, so its reference to this case rests on the county, the timing and the wide distant coverage it described.

reader.title: Reported lynching of Charles Young
bases: Every wire report and the Montgomery Advertiser described a lynching of a Black man accused of an attempted assault on a white woman (A1, A5, A6), though a Birmingham editorial said no lynching took place (A11).

The only reports of a killing were relayed hearsay from Ragland ('a report has reached here') that name no mob, size, method or witness (A1, A5, A6), and the Birmingham Age-Herald stated that the St. Clair county lynching 'did not take place' (A11); the alleged pretext, an attempted assault on a white woman, is stated (A5).

The AP and Birmingham-special reports (A1, A5) and the Montgomery Advertiser (A6) all pass on an unconfirmed report from Coal City, while the Birmingham Age-Herald two days later called the St. Clair county lynching story false (A11).

accounts.gist: A report reaching Ragland from Coal City said Charles Young was lynched Saturday for attempting a criminal assault on Mrs. Barbour, who was alone at home and whose screams frightened him away.

accounts.label: Montgomery Advertiser report
accounts.gist: Young, of a railroad construction gang, went to the Barbour home, asked for something, and finding Mrs. Barbour alone was 'said to have offered insult'; he was chased, found and lynched 'according to the reports'.

accounts.label: Birmingham Age-Herald editorial
accounts.gist: Distant papers carried an account of a lynching in St. Clair county that 'did not take place' and 'was not even considered', blamed on rural reporters anticipating lynchings.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Ragland brief in news-digest columns under heads such as 'Lynched for Attempted Assault', 'Negro Hangs High' and 'The Daily Lynching', taking the accusation as the cause.
The Paducah Sun's head read 'Negro Strung Up for Attempting to Criminally Assault a White Woman', and the Montgomery Advertiser stressed that Mrs. Barbour was the wife of 'a respected citizen'.
The Birmingham Age-Herald denied the lynching and praised Alabama as a 'law-abiding state', attacking the reporters rather than the reported crime or mob.
